value.overview: The Orange-collared Manakin (Manacus aurantiacus) is a small, colorful forest bird of the manakin family. It has a restricted distribution on the Pacific slope of southern Costa Rica and in western Panama. Males gather at traditional display sites, or leks, where they perform courtship displays and produce sharp wing-snapping sounds. Females are less brightly colored and usually remain inconspicuous in dense vegetation. The species is one of the characteristic birds of southwestern Central American lowland forests.
value.classification: The Orange-collared Manakin belongs to the manakin family, Pipridae, and the genus Manacus. It is closely related to the White-collared, Golden-collared, and White-bearded manakins.
value.identification: The Orange-collared Manakin is a compact bird about 10 centimeters long. The adult male has a black crown, back, wings, and tail, with a vivid orange throat, collar, and upper breast, an olive-green rump, and yellowish lower underparts. Females are mainly olive-green above and yellowish below, with no bright orange collar. Males are often detected by their rapid wing snaps and other mechanical display sounds near a forest-floor lek.
value.rangeHabitat: This species occurs from southwestern Costa Rica into western Panama. In Costa Rica, it is found mainly on the Pacific side of the southern and southwestern lowlands and foothills, including areas such as the Osa region, the Golfo Dulce lowlands, and the Carara area. It uses humid lowland and foothill forest, forest edges, secondary growth, and some plantations. Costa Rican records extend from near sea level to roughly 1,100 meters, although it is most characteristic of warm, moist forest habitats.
value.migrationStatus: Resident. Orange-collared Manakins occur year-round in suitable areas of southwestern Costa Rica and western Panama, and there is no reliable evidence of regular long-distance migration. Local movements may occur as birds track fruit resources.
value.breeding: Males gather in communal leks on the forest floor, where they defend small display courts and perform visual and mechanical courtship displays to attract females. Wing snapping is an important part of the display. Females select mates and build the nest and raise the young without male parental care. The nest is a small, open cup placed in low vegetation. Nesting details and the exact breeding season may vary across the species' restricted range.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists primarily of small fruits, especially berries and other fleshy forest fruits. Birds usually forage quietly in the understory and lower canopy, often moving between fruiting plants near display areas. Like other manakins, they may also take small insects and other arthropods, particularly when feeding nestlings or young birds. By swallowing fruits and later passing their seeds, they contribute to seed dispersal in tropical forests.
value.behavior: Orange-collared Manakins are active, agile understory birds that commonly travel short distances between dense cover and fruiting plants. Males spend much of the breeding period near their display courts, competing with neighboring males and performing repeated courtship routines. Females are generally quieter and less conspicuous. The species may occur singly or in small, loose groups at feeding sites, but males become strongly associated with traditional leks during courtship.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not precisely quantified, but the species is not currently considered to be declining rapidly enough to qualify for a threatened category.
